segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Pilate took Jesus and had him flogged.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head, and they put a purple cloak around him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they came up to him again and again, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hail, King of the Jews!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they slapped him in the face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate went outside again and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus came outside, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple cloak. And Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Here is the man!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Crucify! Crucify!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no basis for a charge against him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jewish leaders answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die, because he made himself out to be the Son of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Pilate heard this statement, he grew more afraid,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he went back into the governor’s headquarters and said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where are you from?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus gave him no answer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You would have no authority over me at all if it had not been given to you from above. For this reason the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From then on Pilate tried to release him, but the Jewish leaders shouted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Everyone who makes himself out to be a king opposes Caesar.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside and sat down on the judge’s seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, or in Hebrew, Gabbatha.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now it was the day of Preparation for the Passover, and it was about noon. He said to the Jewish leaders,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Here is your king!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they shouted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Take him away! Take him away! Crucify him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Shall I crucify your king?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have no king but Caesar.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he handed him over to them to be crucified. So they took charge of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Carrying the cross himself, he went out to what is called the Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where they crucified him, and with him two others, one on each side, with Jesus in the middle.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate also had a notice written and put on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many of the Jews read this notice, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not write ‘The King of the Jews,’ but that this man said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What I have written, I have written.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his clothes and divided them into four shares, a share for each soldier; they also took his tunic. Now the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top down.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it will be.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was so that the Scripture would be fulfilled that says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “They divided my clothes among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So that is what the soldiers did.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But standing beside the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, here is your son.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to the disciple,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Here is your mother.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this, knowing that everything was now finished, Jesus said, so that the Scripture would be completed,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am thirsty.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A jar full of sour wine was standing there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop stalk and held it to his mouth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had taken the sour wine, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is finished.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And bowing his head, he handed over his spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day—the Jewish leaders asked Pilate to have their legs broken and the bodies taken away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man and of the other who had been crucified with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead, one of the soldiers stabbed his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who saw it has testified, and his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Not a bone of his will be broken.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again, another Scripture says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “They will look on the one they pierced.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, though a secret one for fear of the Jewish leaders, asked Pilate to let him take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave permission. So he came and took away his body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nicodemus also came, the one who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So because it was the Jews’ day of Preparation, and since the tomb was nearby, they laid Jesus there.

notes.note: The Greek is “the Jews,” the traditional rendering. In John’s trial narrative the group pressing Pilate is the Jerusalem authorities—the chief priests and their officers named in verse 6—not the Jewish people as a whole, so the narrower phrase is used here and in verses 12, 14, 31, and 38. Scholars are divided over the word generally: some prefer “Judeans” throughout, while others object that this removes Jews from the New Testament.

“Friend of Caesar” may be more than a figure of speech: the phrase was used of those who enjoyed the emperor’s recognized favor, and losing that standing could end a career. Whether Pilate formally held such a status is uncertain, but the threat of being reported to the emperor as disloyal is clear.

notes.phrase: sat down on the judge’s seat
notes.traditional: sat down on the judgment seat
notes.note: The Greek verb can also take an object, giving “seated him on the judge’s seat,” so that Pilate places Jesus there in mockery before saying “Here is your king.” Most translators and commentators take it as Pilate himself sitting to pronounce sentence, as here; a minority defend the other reading.

The Greek word means “in the language of the Hebrews” and in this period could cover Aramaic as well as Hebrew. Gabbatha and Golgotha (verse 17) are Aramaic in form, and some versions therefore translate “in Aramaic.”

notes.phrase: the day of Preparation for the Passover
notes.note: “Preparation” was the ordinary name for Friday, the day before the Sabbath (see verse 31). The phrase can mean the day on which the Passover was prepared, that is, the day before the feast, or “the Friday of Passover week.” The first fits John 18:28, where the leaders have not yet eaten the Passover; the second is preferred by those who align John’s chronology with the other Gospels.

The Greek says “about the sixth hour.” Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is midday, whereas the literal phrase suggests six o’clock to a modern reader. A minority of scholars argue that John counts from midnight, partly to ease the difference from Mark 15:25, which puts the crucifixion at the third hour.

notes.phrase: his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene
notes.note: The Greek list can be read as naming four women or three, if “Mary of Clopas” identifies the sister just mentioned. Most scholars count four, since two sisters both named Mary would be unlikely. The Greek says only “Mary of Clopas”; “wife” is the usual inference, though “daughter” is possible.

In Greek this was a normal and courteous way to address a woman, without the curtness the bare word has in English; Jesus addresses his mother the same way at John 2:4. It is nonetheless unusual from a son to his mother, and interpreters differ over what, if anything, it signals.

Most versions have “fulfilled,” but the verb is not John’s usual word for fulfilling Scripture (used in verses 24 and 36); it is related to “finished” in this verse and verse 30 and means to bring to completion. The clause may attach to what follows, as here, with Jesus speaking so that Scripture is completed (Psalm 69:21 is usually suggested), or to what precedes: everything was finished so that Scripture would be completed.

Most versions have “gave up his spirit.” The verb is the same one used throughout the passion narrative for handing Jesus over (verses 11 and 16), and it was not a stock Greek expression for dying; the rendering keeps that link and the sense of a deliberate act. To whom the spirit is handed is not stated; most interpreters understand the Father.

Breaking the legs hastened death; the usual explanation is that the crucified could no longer push themselves up to breathe. The Law required that an executed body not be left hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and this Sabbath was especially solemn because it fell at Passover.

The Greek has an emphatic “that one knows.” It most naturally refers to the eyewitness himself, as rendered here. Some interpreters take “that one” as someone other than the witness—Christ or God—called on to confirm his testimony.

notes.phrase: Not a bone of his will be broken
notes.note: The wording is closest to the rules for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12), though Psalm 34:20, about God guarding the righteous sufferer, is also possible. Many scholars think John intends both; the Passover reference fits the setting of this chapter.

The unit is the Roman pound, roughly a third of a kilogram, so the amount is about thirty-three kilograms, or some seventy-two modern pounds. It is an extravagant quantity, far beyond what an ordinary burial required.

candidates.reason: Versions vary between Praetorium, palace, headquarters and residence across the Gospels, Acts 23:35 and Philippians 1:13, and the loanword tempts translators.
Recurs in Matthew, Acts, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10 as judgment seat, tribunal, bench or court, and readers should see that Pilate’s seat and Christ’s are the same word.
Translations split between “in Hebrew” and “in Aramaic” in John, Acts and Revelation, and the choice should be uniform.
Numbered hours occur across the Gospels and Acts and need one policy: literal “sixth hour” or modern clock equivalents.
Rendered variously as “of Nazareth,” “the Nazarene” or “the Nazorean” across the Gospels and Acts, and Matthew 2:23 depends on the form.
